title: Declare a stable packet capability profile

state.decision_rationale: Rejected as a second capability-negotiation layer. MKTCTX/4 protocol magic, named projection profiles, section statuses, and per-file projections already state the testable guarantees; another profile version would duplicate and risk drifting from them.

provenance.source_label: Grok highest-leverage next step: packet profile
provenance.review_target: MKTCTX/3 Continuum packet; exact artifact not identified

feedback.verbatim: A short, stable packet profile declaration: versioned capabilities the consumer can rely on.
feedback.normalized_claim: Declare a compact, versioned profile or capability set so consumers know which optional structures and guarantees are present.

current_behavior: Protocol magic identifies MKTCTX/3 and records expose their own statuses and projections.
There is no profile name or explicit capability list independent of the protocol version.
Optional manifest, sidecars, task, numbered view, analyzer availability, omissions, and edge status are discoverable from records rather than negotiated up front.
evidence: src/index.ts: CLI format and projection options

proposal.summary: Evaluate whether named profiles should declare consumer-relevant guarantees separately from protocol grammar and per-packet observed statuses.
candidate_changes: Define a compact @profile name and version with normative required and optional capabilities.
Separate promised capabilities from observed analyzer status, selection completeness, and per-file projections.
Allow consumers to reject unsupported required capabilities before scanning the packet.
Align profile naming with future manifest, review, query, and lossless-selection policies only if their semantics are fully specified.
non_goals: Do not duplicate every header and section field into a capabilities list.
Do not let profile names substitute for normative behavior.
Do not imply populated edges merely because the grammar supports an @edges block.

questions: What can a profile promise that the protocol version and existing status records cannot?
Are profiles transport capabilities, selection policies, representation policies, or bundles of all three?
Can profile evolution remain compatible without fragmenting implementations?
Should capability negotiation occur outside the packet instead?
risks: Profiles can become vague marketing names rather than testable contracts.
Overlapping profile and protocol versions increase compatibility complexity.
A capability list can drift from actual emitted records.
evidence_needed: Consumer use cases that cannot cheaply determine support from existing records.
Normative capability matrix with conformance tests.
Compatibility examples across protocol and profile evolution.
Token-cost comparison of profile declarations and current self-description.
